questions.q: Why does this lesson say application boundaries matter on Salesforce even though the platform has no technical wall forcing them?
options: Because Salesforce actually does enforce boundaries automatically between every custom object
Boundaries only matter in multi-org environments, never within a single org
Because without a deliberately drawn boundary, an org can accrete into one undifferentiated mass where no one can confidently say what depends on what
Application boundaries are purely a licensing concept with no architectural consequence
questions.explain: Salesforce's platform makes it easy to keep adding to the same org indefinitely with no enforced wall -- which is exactly why an architect has to deliberately draw boundaries, or the org risks becoming an unmanageable monolith.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three signals this lesson gives that a feature belongs outside its current application boundary?
options: The feature will be maintained by a different team on a different release cadence than the application it's being added to
The feature uses a custom object instead of a standard object
The feature was requested by a vice president rather than a manager
The feature uses Apex instead of Flow
questions.explain: A different owner and different lifecycle/release cadence is one of the three boundary signals -- alongside a different audience with a weak data relationship, and reusability beyond the current context.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what practical benefit does a well-bounded application provide when something breaks?
options: It guarantees the bug will never recur
It automatically fixes the bug without developer involvement
Bounded applications are immune to bugs by design
It narrows where to look, since a well-bounded application has a knowable, limited set of objects, flows, and components
questions.explain: A well-bounded application's knowable scope narrows the search space when debugging, testing a change, or deciding whether a capability can be safely turned off.

questions.q: How does this lesson relate application boundary decisions to Lesson 19 (Packaging and Modularity)?
options: They are unrelated topics covered in completely separate contexts
Drawing the boundary is the conceptual decision made first; packaging (managed/unlocked packages) is the concrete mechanism covered later that enforces a boundary already decided here
Packaging decisions must always be made before any boundary is drawn
Packaging replaces the need to draw application boundaries at all
questions.explain: This lesson deliberately stays conceptual: draw the boundary first based on ownership, audience, and reuse, then Lesson 19 covers how packaging turns that decision into something enforced in deployment tooling.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say none of the three boundary signals is a hard rule by itself?
options: Because the signals contradict each other and can never be used together
Because only the reusability signal actually matters; the other two are irrelevant

Because a small internal tool with one owner and one audience doesn't automatically need its own boundary just because it's technically separable -- the signals are weighed together as a judgment call
Because Salesforce's architecture enforces boundaries automatically regardless of these signals
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as a judgment call weighing all three signals against the cost of managing one more boundary -- not a checklist where any single signal mechanically forces a new boundary.
